title: Apology - Opening Defense
author: Plato
description: Socrates' defense speech at his trial for impiety and corrupting the youth of Athens.

sections.greek: Ὅτι μὲν ὑμεῖς, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, πεπόνθατε ὑπὸ τῶν ἐμῶν κατηγόρων, οὐκ οἶδα· ἐγὼ δ᾽ οὖν καὶ αὐτὸς ὑπ᾽ αὐτῶν ὀλίγου ἐμαυτοῦ ἐπελαθόμην, οὕτω πιθανῶς ἔλεγον. καίτοι ἀληθές γε ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν οὐδὲν εἰρήκασιν.
sections.translation: How you, men of Athens, have been affected by my accusers, I do not know; but I, for my part, almost forgot who I was because of them, so persuasively did they speak. And yet they have said practically nothing true.
grammaticalNotes: ὅτι μέν...ἐγὼ δ᾽ οὖν: balanced contrast between you and I
ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν: parenthetical phrase softening the statement

sections.greek: ἐγὼ δ᾽ οὖν ὑμῖν τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἐρῶ. οὐ μέντοι μὰ Δία, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, κεκαλλιεπημένους γε λόγους, ὥσπερ οἱ τούτων, ῥήμασί τε καὶ ὀνόμασιν οὐδὲ κεκοσμημένους, ἀλλ᾽ ἀκούσεσθε εἰκῇ λεγόμενα τοῖς ἐπιτυχοῦσιν ὀνόμασιν.
sections.translation: But I shall tell you the truth. Not, by Zeus, men of Athens, speeches adorned with fine phrases and words, like theirs, nor embellished, but you will hear things spoken at random in whatever words occur to me.

grammaticalNotes: Socrates contrasts rhetorical style with simple truth
κεκαλλιεπημένους, κεκοσμημένους: perfect participles showing completed states
τοῖς ἐπιτυχοῦσιν ὀνόμασιν: 'with whatever words occur'

sections.greek: πιστεύω γὰρ δίκαια εἶναι ἃ λέγω, καὶ μηδεὶς ὑμῶν προσδοκησάτω ἄλλως· οὐδὲ γὰρ ἂν δήπου πρέποι, ὦ ἄνδρες, τῇδε τῇ ἡλικίᾳ ὥσπερ μειρακίῳ πλάττοντι λόγους εἰς ὑμᾶς εἰσιέναι.
sections.translation: For I believe that what I say is just, and let none of you expect otherwise; for surely it would not be fitting, men, for one of my age to come before you like a youth fashioning speeches.

vocabulary.form: pres act part dat sg m

grammaticalNotes: μηδεὶς προσδοκησάτω: negative imperative with aorist
οὐδὲ γὰρ ἂν πρέποι: potential optative 'it would not be fitting'
τῇδε τῇ ἡλικίᾳ: dative of reference 'for one of this age'

historicalContext: In 399 BCE, Socrates was tried and condemned to death on charges of impiety and corrupting the youth. Plato's Apology presents Socrates' defense speech, offering insight into his philosophical method and moral courage.
literaryFeatures: Ironic contrast between rhetoric and truth
Socrates claims to speak simply while using sophisticated techniques
Direct address to the Athenian jury
Socratic irony: claiming ignorance while demonstrating wisdom
